title: Mosaic: wafer-scale DRAM-on-logic with defective tiles mapped out
idea: Forced 'mosaic': a whole undiced DRAM wafer is bonded face-to-face to a logic wafer, and tiles found bad at test are fused out of a mosaic address map. The result is one wafer-scale memory with no packaging, no PHYs and no dicing between memory and compute.
why: Interface energy and packaging cost; removes PHY/SerDes per die and gives TB/s-class bandwidth per mm of wafer.

title: Contactless smartcard coupling: unbonded face-to-face capacitive memory links
idea: Contactless smartcards exchange data across air gaps. Place memory and logic dies face-to-face across ~1 um of dielectric with arrays of 5 um capacitor plates, signaling with low-voltage pulses and no metallurgical bond or ESD structures.
why: No ESD, no bumps and ~1-5 fF per channel give ~10-50 fJ/bit (>10x below HBM I/O); dies can be tested and swapped before final assembly, avoiding known-good-die losses.

title: Lead-free's chaotic transition fixed: shared qualification bank for abundant materials
idea: The 2006 RoHS lead-free switch went badly (tin whiskers, brittle joints) because each OEM repeated years of reliability testing alone. Fund a pre-competitive U.S. qualification bank, CHIPS-funded and governed by OSATs and hyperscalers, that runs JEDEC thermal-cycle, electromigration and HAST tests once on Earth-abundant packaging materials (Zn-Al joints, Cu-Mn barriers, Cu sinter, AlN dielectrics, ferrite magnetics) and publishes shared data and design rules.
why: Cuts 2-3 years and per-firm cost from qualification, making substitution away from Sn, Ag, In, Ta, W and Co practical for U.S. memory packaging and resilient to chokepoints.

title: Liquid-metal microwell interconnects that never freeze
idea: Po: the solder stays liquid forever. One mask patterns microwells in a polymer layer, a gallium alloy fills them by squeegee, and the mating die's pads dip into the wells, giving fine-pitch joints that absorb thermal mismatch and can be reworked.
why: Removes solder-fatigue and warpage yield loss in large HBM packages and allows reuse of stacks; no reflow heat on DRAM.

title: Segmentation: per-tile 2-high DRAM micro-stacks bonded over compute
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation, resolving 'more bandwidth vs. limited die-edge shoreline': replace 6-8 edge-mounted 12-high HBM stacks with ~64 two-high DRAM micro-stacks hybrid-bonded on top of each compute tile at ~9 um pitch. Each micro-stack feeds only the tile beneath it, and the logic NoC handles sharing.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): wire length drops from ~5 mm to <0.1 mm, so ~3.5 falls to ~0.3 pJ/bit. 2-high stacks avoid compound 12-high yield loss, and shoreline stops limiting bandwidth.

title: Graded-speed DRAM bins packaged into wide slow modules
idea: Substitute prime-only DRAM sourcing with fab speed-reject and down-bin dies, graded on an open-source FPGA DRAM tester and packaged into wide, slow modules where 2x more chips at lower clock deliver the same bandwidth.
why: Supply and cost per bit: dies otherwise scrapped or discounted become usable supply; +5-10% bits at 30-50% lower cost per bit.

title: Undiced wafer-scale memory slabs with route-around redundancy
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Never dice the DRAM wafer: add a top metal mesh that routes around bad reticles, then mount whole 300 mm wafers as a stack of 10 slabs with edge connectors and liquid cooling between slabs.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packages, test sockets and module PCBs (~15-30% of module cost); a 10-wafer slab holds ~10x the bits per rack U of DIMMs at similar cost.

title: Ephaptic coupling: stacked glass memory panels talk through capacitive fields
idea: Neurons in tight bundles influence each other through the shared extracellular field (ephaptic coupling) without synapses. Likewise thin glass panels carrying oxide-TFT memory are stacked with ~2 um polymer spacers, and matching pads on adjacent panels exchange data by capacitive coupling, with no vias or bonds between panels.
why: Removes signal TSVs and through-glass vias, allows field-replaceable panel stacks, ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical I/O over um gaps, and uses glass instead of silicon wafers.

title: MacEtch TSVs whose catalyst becomes the plating seed
idea: Combine metal-assisted chemical etching with via metallization: a perforated Au/Ag catalyst film sinks into silicon in HF/H2O2 at room temperature, carving 50-100 um vertical holes, and the same catalyst left at the via bottom serves as the seed for bottom-up Cu electroplating after an electrografted polymer liner. No Bosch DRIE (helium backside cooling) and no argon-sputtered seed.
why: TSV cost and rare-gas exposure: removes both rare-gas-dependent TSV steps and a costly plasma tool; claims 40-60% lower TSV module cost on U.S.-friendly wet benches.

title: Fridge magnet: magnetic self-alignment for low-cost chiplet assembly
idea: Like a fridge magnet snapping into place: dies get patterned Ni/Co pads and are dropped onto a substrate over a patterned magnet fixture that pulls each die to sub-micron alignment, then bonded in a batch oven, with no $5M placement tool.
why: Packaging capital intensity; fine-pitch memory-logic assembly on cheap equipment and a U.S.-friendly assembly route.

title: Cryo-EM style LN2 memory drawer at 0.4 V and 50 mV swing
idea: Cryo-EM and magnet labs already handle LN2 routinely. Immerse whole memory drawers in liquid nitrogen: at 77 K subthreshold swing ~20 mV/dec lets periphery run at ~0.4 V and links at ~50 mV, copper resistance falls ~7x, and access-transistor leakage collapses so refresh nearly stops.
why: CV2 per access ~8-10x lower and refresh (~46 fJ/bit idle) vanishes at the memory; cryocooler overhead (~3-10 W/W) eats much of it, so net only wins with cheap industrial LN2 (~1.5-3x).

title: Acoustic through-die links from U.S. FBAR piezo transducers
idea: Invert 'vertical data must flow as electrons': place AlN/ScAlN thin-film bulk-acoustic transducers (made in a Colorado FBAR fab) on each die and send GHz acoustic pulses straight through bonded silicon to a receiver on the next die.
why: No TSVs, holes or optics; ~50 um transducers at ~1-5 Gb/s each let stacks skip the TSV tax with a fully domestic supply chain.

title: Thermomigrated aluminum trails form TSVs with no etching
idea: Combine solar-cell thermal-gradient zone melting with through-silicon vias: print Al dots on an n-type wafer and apply a vertical temperature gradient (IR heating below, chilled plate above) so molten Al-Si droplets migrate through the wafer, leaving Al-saturated p+ columns (~1-2 ohm each) junction-isolated from the bulk.
why: TSV capital: no DRIE (helium cooling), no liner/barrier/seed PVD (argon), no plating; claims 5-10x cheaper vias for power/ground and slow signals.

title: Skipping: DRAM dies overhang compute edge, bonded face-to-face, no interposer
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping (rush through the harmful stage): skip the interposer by bonding each DRAM die face-to-face onto a 1.5 mm strip along the compute die edge. The rest of the DRAM die is cantilevered over a mold shelf that carries its power vias.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and the CoWoS capacity chokepoint: no interposer and no data TSVs, for ~0.3 pJ/bit links.

title: Capacitive kiss pads for removable DRAM-on-logic stacking
idea: Po: memory and logic touch without bonding. A single added mask patterns thin-passivated capacitive plates on the DRAM top metal; the die is pressed face-to-face onto matching logic plates with no metal bond, so signals cross by capacitive coupling and the die can be removed.
why: Gives HBM-class density with zero bonding yield loss and full rework; KGD problem disappears.

title: Bank-under-tile: each compute tile owns the DRAM bank beneath it
idea: Worsen: route every bit across a shared bus to a DIMM 10 cm away. Flip: hybrid-bond DRAM face-to-face onto logic at ~1 um pitch so each compute tile talks only to the bank directly below it through thousands of vertical wires, with no PHY, no shared bus and no SerDes.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): wire length drops from cm to <50 um, ~3 pJ/bit to ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit; PHY periphery area removed from both dies.

title: Wide I/O reborn on backside-power SoCs: memory bonded to freed frontside
idea: JEDEC Wide I/O died because ~1,200 TSVs had to pierce the hot, expensive SoC die, and phone vendors refused the yield, area and test hit. With backside power delivery (PowerVia/A16-class), the SoC's power and I/O exit through its back, so a thinned DRAM die can be hybrid-bonded face-to-face onto the SoC frontside at 3-9 um pitch with zero TSVs in either die, with refresh rate set from the logic die's thermal sensors.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): face-to-face bonds at ~0.05 pJ/bit vs ~4-5 pJ/bit for LPDDR5X, roughly 50-100x less I/O energy; removes the TSV tax (fact 6) and the package PHY area.

title: 77 K superconducting REBCO interposer frees HBM from beachfront
idea: Extreme user: MRI and fusion-magnet labs that run HTS tape at 77 K. Pattern REBCO thin-film transmission lines on a sapphire/MgO interposer held at 77 K by a closed-cycle cooler; lossless, near-dispersion-free lines let 16-32 HBM-class stacks sit 5-20 cm from the GPU instead of crowding its edge, with no retimers or equalizers.
why: Breaks the shoreline/beachfront limit (~8 stacks per GPU) and the interposer reticle limit; 2-4x memory capacity per accelerator at similar pJ/bit; generalizes to any cryo-cooled AI rack.

title: One optical copy of weights broadcast to a hundred accelerators
idea: First principles: read-only weights need O(1) storage, not O(N) copies, if broadcast bandwidth exists. Keep one model copy in a central memory node and stream it in layer order through a passive 1:128 optical splitter tree to accelerators running in lockstep; each holds only a few-layer SRAM ring buffer.
why: Weight GB per accelerator falls ~100x, so cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades scheduling flexibility (all nodes run the same layer at once).

title: Superconducting persistent-current loops behind an optical cryostat window
idea: Ideal: a current that circulates forever with no supply. Closest achievable: store bits as flux quanta in niobium persistent-current loops at 4 K (Josephson memory arrays) driven by on-cryostat SFQ logic, with data entering and leaving through optical fiber links to warm processors.
why: Zero refresh and zero static power at the cell with aJ-class writes; costs are cryocooler power, poor cell density and closed-cycle helium use, which conflicts with the helium chokepoint.

title: One end-to-end code spanning DRAM array ECC and link FEC
idea: Combine on-die ECC with the interface's link CRC/FEC: compute one strong RS/LDPC code over the line plus metadata at write time, store its parity in the array, and transmit stored parity over the link unchanged so the host corrects array and channel errors in a single decode.
why: Periphery and I/O energy: deletes on-die ECC logic (~3-5% die area) and duplicate link ECC; tolerating link BER ~1e-6 permits lower swing for ~20-30% I/O energy savings.

title: Paper airplane: bit-plane layout so reads fetch only needed precision
idea: A paper airplane flies with only what it needs: weights are stored transposed into bit-planes, so a 4-bit inference pass reads only the top 4 planes of FP16 weights over the link. Implemented as a controller and layout change on an FPGA prototype.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth: 2-4x fewer bits moved per inference, and one stored copy serves many precisions.

title: One end-to-end ECC codeword from cell to core
idea: Worsen: re-encode data at every hop, with on-die ECC, link CRC, controller ECC and cache ECC each adding bits and latency. Flip: generate one strong codeword when data enters the array, ship its raw parity bits over the link and decode only once in the processor, deleting link and on-die ECC logic.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and bandwidth: ~6-12% bandwidth and several % of die area recovered; one stronger code tolerates weaker cells and relaxes refresh.

title: Refresh-by-migration: refresh rows by moving them to their next tier
idea: Fuse the 64 ms refresh timescale with the tiering timescale: instead of activating rows only to rewrite them in place, the controller reads rows due for refresh out over the link and writes them to their new home (hot rows up toward on-package, cold rows down to pooled memory). Mandated refresh activations become free migration bandwidth.
why: Converts ~46 fJ/bit refresh spend (fact 3) into useful placement work and cuts separate migration traffic by ~30-50% in tiered memory systems.

title: 1990s VCSEL ribbon optics disaggregate memory onto rack shelves
idea: Adapted from 1990s 12-channel 850 nm VCSEL parallel-optics datacom modules on multimode ribbon: memory moves to dedicated shelves linked to compute by many slow parallel VCSEL lanes, with driver and receiver chips at 180 nm or larger.
why: Raises usable supply through pooling and moves DRAM away from hot accelerators; mature GaAs VCSEL lines give ~5-10 pJ/bit at 2.5 Gb/s lanes, fine for capacity tiers.

title: Millisecond DRAM: tiny capacitors legal because data dies young
idea: Ideal: a capacitor that stores just enough charge for exactly as long as needed. Closest achievable: specify a die class with ~1 fF cells (aspect ratio ~15:1 instead of 60-75:1) guaranteed for only ~2 ms retention, sold exclusively behind a TTL/streaming interface that refuses allocations longer than 1 ms, so it is never refreshed.
why: Fact 1 capacitor wall and fact 4: shallow capacitors drop the costliest etch and deposition steps, raise yield and allow ~1.5-2x density at the same node, with refresh energy zero by contract.

title: Cu-Mn self-forming barrier, failed in fine lines, revived for TSVs
idea: Cu-Mn alloy seeds that self-form a MnSiO barrier on anneal were dropped from advanced BEOL because residual Mn raised resistivity in 20 nm lines, a penalty that vanishes in 2-10 um TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and contact plugs. Use Cu-0.5%Mn seed in HBM TSVs, hybrid-bond pads and base-die contact plugs to eliminate Ta/TaN barriers and W plugs; the 2-3 nm self-formed barrier also frees TSV diameter.
why: Removes Ta (conflict-region supply) and W (China ~80%) from the memory interconnect stack and cuts PVD steps (capital) and TSV stress; Cu and Mn only.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling replaces helium in TSV plasma etch
idea: Combine the electrostatic chuck's backside gas cooling with hydrogen, whose thermal conductivity (~0.18 W/m-K) beats helium's (~0.15), using a low-leak sealed chuck with H2 sensing and interlocks so TSV DRIE and other plasma steps keep wafer temperature control with no helium; H2 is made domestically by electrolysis.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps HBM TSV etch lines running independent of helium supply.

title: RDRAM's royalty trap fixed: royalty-free open memory-PHY commons for newcomers
idea: Rambus RDRAM lost partly because per-chip royalties, litigation and costly at-speed test made it pricier than SDRAM. Create a RISC-V-style foundation that funds, silicon-proves and licenses royalty-free DRAM-side PHYs, TSV/hybrid-bond I/O cells and controller IP, backed by a defensive patent pool of CHIPS-Act buyers, so a U.S. memory or packaging startup can tape out a base die without a $10-30M IP bill.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: removes tens of $M and months from entry, and blunts the litigation risk that killed earlier memory-interface startups.

title: GaN-on-diamond radar trick: diamond interlayers enable 32-high stacks
idea: Military radars bond GaN to CVD diamond to dump extreme heat flux. Insert 20-50 um CVD-diamond spreader layers every four DRAM dies, with laser-cut windows for TSVs, carrying heat sideways to a side-wall cold plate.
why: Thermal resistance caps HBM at ~12-16 high; diamond (~2000 W/mK, lab-grown in the US) allows ~32-high stacks, ~2x bits per footprint without denser cells.

title: Projector micromirror chips switch light between memory and hosts
idea: Substitute the electrical CXL switch with a free-space optical crossbar built from a commodity DLP micromirror array that steers fiber-collimated beams between memory sleds and servers; kHz reconfiguration is enough for circuit-switched memory pooling.
why: Utilization: memory reassignable across 32-64 hosts over passive, low-energy optical paths built from cheap consumer parts.

title: Ba: barium-titanate Pockels modulators for femtojoule memory optics
idea: Bond thin-film epitaxial BaTiO3 (r42 ~900 pm/V, ~30x LiNbO3) onto silicon microrings so memory-link modulators switch with ~0.5 V and ~10 fF, driven directly from DRAM-process logic without driver amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): optical memory I/O with ~50-100 fJ/bit modulator energy, making off-package memory cheaper per bit moved than HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit.

title: Wavelength is the address: bank-per-color photonic interposer
idea: Scarcity: no address decode logic on the memory die. A silicon-nitride photonic interposer gives each DRAM bank a fixed WDM wavelength via a tuned microring drop filter; a request is a pulse on that bank's color and the reply returns on the same color, so routing and arbitration happen optically.
why: Cuts address/command periphery (fact 7) and long electrical routes (fact 5); 32-64 wavelengths x 25 Gb/s per waveguide targets ~1-2 pJ/bit at cm reach.

title: Laser-sliced active layers replace backgrinding and save donor wafers
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x hybrid-bond stack x reusable donor wafer x dry laser subsurface slicing. A laser-focused cleave plane 40 um under the device layer lets the finished DRAM layer split off dry, skipping water-cooled backgrinding and polish; the remaining wafer is plasma-smoothed and reused for another DRAM layer.
why: Water: backgrind/polish coolant and rinses are a top packaging water draw; dry cleave plus plasma cuts that >10x. Also cuts virgin silicon and quartz-crucible demand (Spruce Pine chokepoint) by reusing donors 5-10x.

title: MicroLED imaging-fiber links make cheap DDR act like HBM
idea: Box: commodity DDR5 die x standard access x standard SA x 300-lane microLED/CMOS-photodiode array x coherent imaging fiber bundle x flip-chip GaN-on-Si chiplet. Each lane is a blue microLED at ~2 Gb/s imaged pixel-to-pixel through the bundle, so a buffer chip next to commodity DRAM delivers HBM-class aggregate bandwidth at <1 pJ/bit over 1-5 m.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): substitutes DDR (about 1/3 the wafer area per bit of HBM) for HBM while keeping bandwidth, and lets memory live outside the hot package.

title: Sewing-needle stack-then-drill one via through all sixteen dies
idea: Bond the thinned dies first, then deep-etch or laser-drill one via through the whole stack, like a needle through layered cloth, and plate it in one pass. Each die only needs a landing ring, not its own TSV module.
why: Removes per-die TSV processing and compound yield loss; claims ~50% lower HBM stacking cost.

title: Bond-then-drill: one etch wires a 64-tier wafer stack
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Fusion-bond 64 DRAM wafers thinned to 5 um each (oxide bonding, <100 nm alignment), then pattern once and etch/fill vertical buses through the whole stack like a 3D-NAND channel hole, so one litho step and one deep etch replace 63 separate TSV and bump steps.
why: TSV/bump cost (fact 6) is amortized across tiers: 64 thin tiers vs 8-12 in HBM gives ~10x bits per footprint and volume while per-tier interconnect cost drops ~50x.

title: Solar-calculator near-threshold: 100,000 slow lanes at 0.3 V
idea: Solar calculators run for decades at near-threshold voltage by being slow. Use fine-pitch hybrid bonding to give memory 50-100k lanes at only 200-400 Mb/s each, so drivers and receivers run at 0.3 V with no equalization, termination or SerDes.
why: Switching energy scales with V2: 0.3 V lanes vs ~1.1 V I/O give ~13x lower energy at equal aggregate bandwidth; parallelism replaces frequency.

title: Series voltage-stacked DRAM dies slash power-TSV current
idea: Power TSVs and bumps exist to carry current, and I^2R loss and electromigration scale with current, not power. Run four stacked dies in series from a 4.4 V rail, each floating in its own 1.1 V domain, with small switched-capacitor balancers absorbing activity mismatch, so the stack draws one quarter of the current through one quarter of the power vias.
why: Frees ~30-50% of HBM TSVs (much of the array is power/ground) for data or area savings and cuts PDN loss ~16x per via (facts 6, 5).

title: Coal miner's canary: sacrificial early-failure sensors for each memory link
idea: The canary dies first and warns the miners: each package includes intentionally weakened replica bonds, TSVs and lines (narrower, at higher current) that fail first under the same 125 C stress and trigger proactive remapping or service.
why: Gives predictive, calibrated wear-out warning instead of field failures, which allows less over-design (fewer redundant TSVs and less area) while meeting the 10 year/125 C guarantee.

title: Magnetosome chains: field-aligned nanoparticle vias without drilling
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria line magnetite crystals into chains. Here a polymer underfill loaded with gold-shelled Ni/Fe3O4 nanoparticles is cured under a vertical magnetic field, so the particles self-assemble into conductive columns at 1-3 um pitch between stacked dies, with no TSV etch, no microbump and no fine-pitch alignment.
why: Capital intensity and TSV tax (fact 6): removes deep-etch and bumping steps; aims at ~10x denser vertical I/O than microbumps at a fraction of hybrid-bonding tool cost.

title: Simultaneous bidirectional DQ: reads and writes share each wire
idea: Eliminate bus turnaround and half the data pins: both ends drive each on-package lane at once and subtract their own known transmitted signal with a hybrid echo canceller (as gigabit Ethernet does), so reads and writes flow concurrently on the same wire.
why: Removes tWTR/tRTW bubbles (~10-15% bandwidth loss on mixed traffic) and allows halving DQ count or doubling bandwidth per mm of beachfront.

title: Lichen symbiosis: convert display-glass TFT lines into memory interposer fabs
idea: A lichen joins a fungus and an alga that pool their strengths. Glass makers team with idle Gen-6 to Gen-8.5 LCD/OLED TFT lines, which already pattern oxide and metal on huge glass sheets, to make glass-panel interposers and IGZO routing layers for memory packages, adding only laser via drilling and copper plating.
why: Capital intensity and time-to-capacity: reuses depreciated display tooling at panel scale (~10x wafer area per tool); a U.S. variant pairs domestic glass producers with new panel lines for packaging capacity in under 2 years.

title: Photonic base die turns HBM into a fiber-attached appliance
idea: Substitute the HBM base die's electrical PHY with a silicon-photonics base die (microring modulators, Ge detectors, fiber V-grooves), so a stack talks over fiber at ~1 pJ/bit and can sit anywhere on a board or rack.
why: Facts 5/6: frees GPU shoreline and interposer area; memory scales independently of compute and can be pooled for higher utilization.

title: Light-through-silicon vias: 1310 nm optical bus vertically through stack
idea: Combine silicon's transparency at 1310 nm with HBM die stacking: keep small metal-free windows in each ~30 um thinned die and place a wavelength-selective vertical grating coupler plus ring modulator/Ge detector at each window, so a single WDM beam injected from the base die rises through all 12-16 dies and each die drops/adds its own wavelength. Photons replace most data TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (~3x area/bit, 20-30% yield loss): replacing 1,000+ data TSVs with a few optical windows cuts stacking area overhead and TSV-related yield loss, enabling >16-high stacks.

title: Infrared through-silicon optical vias replace TSV stacks
idea: Eliminate copper vias: silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so each thinned die carries Ge photodiodes and micro-emitters in metal-free windows; beams pass straight through intervening dies to receivers on the target die, addressed by position or wavelength.
why: Removes TSV area, via reveal, stress keep-out zones and TSV-driven stack yield loss (HBM TSV tax); no capacitive load on vertical links, claimed <0.5 pJ/bit vertical.

title: Through-silicon light: vertical optical links across IR-transparent dies
idea: Invert 'vertical connections need metal TSVs': silicon is transparent at 1310 nm, so each thinned die carries small emitters and Ge photodiodes in metal-free windows and data beams straight up the stack, die to die, with no holes drilled.
why: Removes TSV etch/fill, keep-out zones and their 20-30% yield hit; each window carries 10-25 Gb/s so ~100 windows replace ~1000 TSVs.

title: Fractional-reserve memory banking with a CXL reserve pool
idea: A bank keeps only part of its deposits as cash. Servers likewise promise more DRAM than they hold, and a rack CXL pool acts as the reserve. A telemetry-driven 'reserve ratio' sets how much local DRAM backs promised capacity. When a run starts, a 'lender of last resort' compresses cold pages to a swap tier.
why: Cloud DRAM is often 40-60% stranded or idle. Overcommit backed by a pooled reserve could cut DRAM bought per server by 20-35% at the same SLA.

title: Ti: rutile-TiO2 trench decoupling under the HBM PHY
idea: Line interposer and base-die deep-trench capacitors with rutile TiO2 (k~80-110, templated on RuO2) instead of HfO2/ZrO2 (k~25-40), tripling decap density directly under the HBM PHY and TSV power columns.
why: Speed-bin yield at an unchanged HBM interface: supply droop is a leading reason stacks miss top speed; ~3x decap cuts droop and could raise good-stack output ~5-10%.

title: Wireless NoC fixed: sealed package cavity broadcasts DRAM commands at 300 GHz
idea: On-chip wireless networks died because tiny antennas radiated poorly into lossy silicon and multipath was unpredictable. Make the package lid and substrate a sealed metal cavity tuned as a 300 GHz waveguide, so on-die antennas on every DRAM die and the controller share a predictable, low-loss broadcast medium for command/address and clock (low-rate, all-to-all), while data stays on wires.
why: Removes command/address TSVs, wires and fan-out buffers in stacks and modules (facts 6, 7), so dies can be added without rerouting; claimed 10-20% fewer TSVs and lower C/A power.

title: Gecko-foot probes test hybrid-bond pads without damage
idea: Gecko feet grip with millions of soft setae. A contactor of metal-coated polymer micro-pillars, molded at room temperature, touches fragile hybrid-bonding pads gently for at-speed known-good-die test. It then lets go, leaving no scratch or particle.
why: Hybrid-bond surfaces can't be probed conventionally, so bad dies get stacked. True KGD test could recover a large part of HBM's 20-30% stacking yield loss.

title: Twelve volts into the stack, per-die switched-capacitor converters
idea: Substitute hundreds of low-voltage power/ground TSVs with a few TSVs carrying 12 V; each DRAM die steps down locally with a switched-capacitor converter built from the DRAM process's own high-density trench capacitors.
why: Fact 6: power/ground TSVs are often >50% of all TSVs; cutting them ~10x shrinks TSV area, lifts stack yield and cuts IR drop for 16-24-high stacks.

title: Hash-deduplicating base die stores shared KV prefixes once
idea: Worsen: store the same system-prompt KV cache separately for every user. Flip: the memory base die hashes each 4 KB block on write and keeps a content-addressed table, so identical prefix blocks across users map to one physical copy with copy-on-write, transparent to the host.
why: Usable capacity: 2-5x more effective KV capacity per GB for chat inference with shared prompts and agents.

title: Tattoo: aerosol-jet printed die-to-die bridges across chiplet gaps
idea: Forced 'tattoo ink': an aerosol-jet printer writes 20 um-pitch silver/copper traces over a printed dielectric ramp directly across the gap between a memory die and a logic die placed on a plain substrate, replacing silicon bridges. Tool rental or a ~$500k tool fits the budget.
why: Capital intensity: maskless chiplet interconnect at a fraction of bridge or interposer cost, buildable in any U.S. lab.

title: Second-life HBM: laser-debond retired stacks into CXL memory cards
idea: Stretch the stack's timescale from a 3-year accelerator life to 10 years: retired accelerators have their HBM laser-debonded, re-bumped and mounted on a cheap organic carrier beside a small CXL controller ASIC that speaks the HBM PHY. Each card becomes a 100+ GB pooled memory device.
why: Adds usable supply with no wafers: millions of HBM stacks retire each year, and reuse costs a small fraction of new bits.

title: Cu: copper-pillar bare DRAM dies soldered straight onto motherboards
idea: Flip-chip unpackaged DRAM dies with Cu pillars directly onto a motherboard region beside the CPU (chip-on-board, glob-topped), eliminating the BGA substrate, DIMM PCB and connector so memory traces shrink from ~10 cm to ~2 cm.
why: Cost per bit and energy: package/module overhead is ~10-15% of DIMM cost and long traces dominate DDR's 10-20 pJ/bit; ~2x lower I/O energy and no substrate supply dependency.

title: Si: anodized porous-silicon interposer cuts HBM link capacitance
idea: Electrochemically anodize the top 50-100 um of the silicon interposer into mesoporous Si (~60% porosity, k~2-3, very high effective resistivity) before building the RDL, so HBM-to-logic traces sit on a near-air dielectric instead of SiO2 over lossy doped Si. Anodization is a maskless wet bath step that fits existing 65 nm-class interposer lines.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~30-40% lower line capacitance and substrate loss, interposer I/O ~0.5 -> ~0.3 pJ/bit and ~2x reach so 12+ HBM stacks can ring one accelerator.

title: Injection-molded liquid-metal vertical channels for reworkable stacks
idea: Mold the stack's encapsulant with micro-channels, then inject gallium-indium alloy like injection molding to form vertical bus lines between barrier-lined pads. A bad die can be removed by heating and vacuuming out the metal, then replaced.
why: Rework turns scrapped 12-high stacks into good ones, attacking the 20-30% HBM yield loss; self-healing joints under thermal cycling.

title: Open UCIe memory-chiplet standard lets any logic fab make memory
idea: Worsen: let memory supply depend on three firms because only they can build the capacitor. Flip: publish an open memory-chiplet standard (UCIe-based protocol, bump map, test and thermal envelope) for capacitorless dies such as SRAM, gain-cell, ROM and flash, so mid-size logic fabs can sell interchangeable memory chiplets.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply: brings dozens of logic fabs into memory supply and makes them compete on cost per bit.

title: Jigsaw-puzzle chiplet edges triple die-to-die shoreline
idea: Use room-temperature plasma dicing to cut memory and compute chiplets with interlocking jigsaw or crenellated edges. Mating pieces meet along a meandering seam that is bridged by short fine-pitch RDL or edge-coupled links.
why: Shoreline caps memory bandwidth. A 3x longer seam on the same die area gives ~3x the die-to-die wires at the same short reach and pJ/bit.

title: Stream seeds, not weights: on-die regeneration of model tensors
idea: Substitute dense weight transfers from HBM with PRNG seeds plus small low-rank/sparse residuals; an LFSR engine on the compute die regenerates the pseudo-random basis and the residual corrects it, so each 64 B of weights crosses the link as ~8-16 B.
why: Fact 5: bytes moved per token and weight capacity both drop ~4-8x for compressible layers.

title: Quantum-computer SFQ pulse links to a 4 K memory
idea: Quantum computers already run single-flux-quantum logic at 4 K to drive qubits. Build the memory interface and periphery in energy-efficient SFQ, where a bit is one flux quantum (~1e-19 J), paired with a cryogenic DRAM array whose leakage is essentially zero.
why: Interface energy per bit falls 100-1000x and refresh disappears; aimed at cryo AI/quantum hybrids where the 4 K budget is already paid, then cryo datacenter pods.

title: Phase-change heat-sponge interlayers enable 24-high stacks for burst seconds
idea: Use the thermal timescale (seconds) as a design variable: thin sealed micro-cells of low-melt Bi-In alloy between DRAM dies melt during training bursts and refreeze during communication lulls. Peaks are buffered rather than conducted, so taller stacks stay within temperature limits.
why: Stack height is thermally capped; 24-high instead of 12-16-high raises GB per package footprint ~1.5-2x without more interposer beachfront (fact 6).

title: Nano-TSVs through 5 um thinned DRAM dies
idea: MINIFY die thickness to ~5 um with backside-power-style wafer thinning so TSVs shrink to 0.5 um diameter, the size of ordinary vias, and the keep-out zone shrinks about 100x.
why: HBM TSV tax: TSV area overhead falls from ~5-10% to <0.5% and stress-related yield loss falls; claims ~15% more bits per stack wafer.

title: Grid-flexible datacenters: non-volatile memory lets racks drop at peaks
idea: Eliminate the 'stay powered to keep state' requirement: with NV working memory, racks cut to zero power within milliseconds on utility demand-response signals and resume exactly where they were; policy lets utilities fast-track interconnection for certified interruptible NV-equipped load.
why: Grid power is now the binding constraint on new AI capacity; interruptible load connects years sooner and needs far less UPS battery, freeing capital and energy.

title: Twenty-millivolt bitline-style die-to-die links bounded by kT/C
idea: The true floor on signal swing is thermal noise sqrt(kT/C), ~0.2 mV rms on a 100 fF bonded link, so 20 mV still gives >10 sigma margin. Replace 0.4 V HBM drivers with charge-dump transmitters and cross-coupled latch receivers clocked like a DRAM sense amp (precharge, share, regenerate), with per-lane offset trim stored at boot.
why: Energy ~C*VDD*dV falls ~20x versus 0.4 V swing: HBM 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.2 pJ/bit (fact 5), and smaller I/O cells shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: 600 mm glass panel interposers with embedded silicon memory bridges
idea: Jump the interposer from a 300 mm wafer to a 600x600 mm glass panel: through-glass vias and multilevel RDL are made on LCD-fab tools, and small silicon bridges are embedded only under the HBM-to-logic edges. One panel yields ~5x the interposer area of a wafer at LCD-class cost per m2.
why: Cuts 2.5D packaging cost and capital ~3-5x with tools that are not EUV-bound and can be built in the U.S.

title: Cell-to-wire PAM: 2-bit analog cells drive the link undigitized
idea: Collapse two signaling scales into one: each cell holds four charge levels, and the sense path forwards its level directly as a PAM-4 symbol over the short hybrid-bonded link, where the host slicer makes the only decision. Cell and link noise merge into one 1% symbol-error budget decoded once.
why: ~2x bits per cell, sidestepping the charge wall (fact 1) by tolerating level errors, and half the wire transitions per bit (~40% less interface energy).

title: Postsynaptic-register signaling: wires toggle only on surprise
idea: Each HBM data lane keeps a 'postsynaptic' predictor latch at the receiver mirrored at the sender (last value per lane per burst position, updated identically at both ends like a Hebbian trace). The sender fires a release pulse only when the real bit differs from the prediction, so steady bit positions such as exponents, sign bits and zero-padding never toggle the wire.
why: Interface pJ/bit (fact 5): ML tensors have strong per-bit-position redundancy; claim 30-50% fewer wire transitions on HBM/DDR links, i.e. 30-50% I/O energy cut with no change to DRAM cells.

title: Fiber-drawing towers produce thousand-wire flexible memory ribbons
idea: Adapted from optical-fiber drawing: a macroscopic polymer preform embedded with copper rods is heated and drawn 100x thinner into kilometers of ribbon. Each ribbon holds thousands of insulated micro-wires at ~20 um pitch and links processor to memory away from the package.
why: Interposer area and adjacency limit: more DRAM can surround a processor through dense wide-slow buses at ~1 pJ/bit and very low cost per wire-meter.

title: Plated-wire looms weave copper interposer fabric instead of silicon CoWoS
idea: Revive the 1960s plated-wire memory weaving looms to weave 15-25 um insulated copper wires at ~40 um pitch into a fabric that is laminated into an organic panel and laser-opened at die sites, forming long memory-to-logic links.
why: Fact 6 and capital: silicon-interposer (CoWoS) capacity is a chokepoint; woven round wire has ~10x lower resistance per mm than 1 um RDL, so HBM can sit 20-50 mm away (more stacks per GPU) on loom-class capital (~$1M) instead of a fab line.

title: Honeybees fan the hive: thin-film thermoelectric cooler under DRAM
idea: Worker bees fan to cool the brood: embed a thin-film Bi2Te3 thermoelectric cooler in the interposer directly under the DRAM stack only, pumping it 15-20 C below the 125 C package while the logic runs hot.
why: DRAM at ~105 C instead of 125 C has about 4x longer retention, so it needs about 4x less refresh energy and loses less bandwidth; the TEC power is spent only on the memory footprint.

title: Sub-THz plastic waveguides for meter-scale memory links
idea: MAGNIFY carrier frequency to ~300 GHz and carry memory traffic over cheap polymer dielectric waveguides (~100 Gb/s per lane) from shared memory boxes up to 1-2 m away, with no lasers.
why: Interposer/CoWoS capacity and stranded memory: memory leaves the package at ~1-2 pJ/bit; pooling raises usable supply by ~20-30%.

title: Phantom-circuit revival: center-tapped third channel rides two differential pairs
idea: Like 1880s telephone phantom circuits, encode a third data stream as the common-mode difference between two differential pairs, injected and recovered through center-tapped terminations, on memory SerDes and package traces.
why: 1.5x bandwidth per wire on differential memory links (CXL/SerDes), so fewer package pins and substrate layers per TB/s; modest energy overhead, common-mode noise is the risk.

title: Molten-salt ion exchange writes waveguides inside glass interposers
idea: Box: DRAM chiplets with grating couplers x standard x photodiodes x buried graded-index waveguides x glass interposer x dry molten KNO3/AgNO3 ion exchange through a laser-ablated metal mask. Waveguides form by ion exchange in a molten salt bath, with no water anywhere, and carry memory traffic across the package.
why: Water: replaces wet silicon-interposer processing, >10x less; optical package links at <1 pJ/bit.

title: Toll booth: HBM base-die-as-a-service, disaggregated stack supply chain
idea: The 'toll booth' is the gate at the road's entry, and the HBM base logic die is the gate to the stack. Standardize the base die-to-core die interface so a logic foundry makes base dies and any vendor's core DRAM dies can be stacked on them at a U.S. OSAT. The base die becomes a separately sourced, competitively bid part.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supplier concentration; opens HBM assembly to new entrants and moves the logic-heavy periphery onto cheaper logic wafers.

title: Peltier effect: thin-film thermoelectric base die cools taller HBM stacks
idea: Embed thin-film Bi2Te3/Sb2Te3 Peltier couples in the HBM base die under hot spots, actively pumping heat out of the DRAM core layers into the cold plate, so 16-24-high stacks stay within thermal limits at the normal 64 ms refresh rate.
why: HBM height ceiling (density per footprint, fact 6) and refresh (fact 3): spends a few W of TEC power for 30-50% more bits per stack.

title: Phonon bandgap: superlattice thermal barrier lets DRAM sit atop hot logic
idea: Insert a 50-100 nm WSe2/MoS2 van der Waals stack or W/Al2O3 nanolaminate with cross-plane thermal conductivity <0.1 W/mK between logic and DRAM, while copper thermal pillars route logic heat sideways; DRAM stays below 85 C despite face-to-face 3D bonding.
why: Enables DRAM-on-logic with the shortest wires (<0.2 pJ/bit, fact 5) without the 2x refresh penalty above 85 C (fact 3).

title: Significance split: MSBs in static cells, LSBs allowed to fade
idea: Ideal: protect only the bits that matter. Closest achievable: the base die bit-slices each fp8/bf16 word so sign, exponent and top mantissa bits go to on-logic SRAM while low mantissa bits go to never-refreshed DRAM, where decay toward zero acts as graceful rounding noise for neural-network tensors.
why: Fact 3: zero refresh power with bounded numerical error (<0.5% relative per decayed value); ~50-60% of bits live in cheap DRAM and the rest in SRAM already present on the base die.

title: Sub-THz plastic waveguides lost to optics; In/Ga bans flip that
idea: Polymer dielectric waveguides carrying 100-300 GHz carriers lost to optical cables because lasers were cheaper at volume. With In/Ga-based lasers ruled out, use solid polyethylene or PTFE ribbons fed by CMOS sub-THz transceivers to connect compute sleds to memory sleds at 1-3 m, carrying 100+ Gb/s per ribbon at ~1-2 pJ/bit with no lasers.
why: Rack-scale memory pooling reclaims the 20-30% of server DRAM that sits stranded, without lasers that need In or Ga; materials are C, H, F, Si and Cu.

title: Package lid as a sub-THz broadcast waveguide
idea: Reverse the heat spreader's role: the copper lid and a substrate ground plane form a parallel-plate waveguide, and each chiplet has a slot antenna radiating 100-300 GHz into it, so one memory chiplet can broadcast a read to many compute chiplets at once without routed wires.
why: Multicast data movement (fact 5): one transmission serves N receivers for weight broadcast, and substrate routing layers are freed.

title: Capacitive proximity tiles aligned by micro-magnets
idea: MINIFY the gap to a ~1 um dielectric: memory tiles clamp face-to-face with compute and signal through capacitive coupling pads at 10 um pitch, aligned by patterned micro-magnets; unclamp to replace.
why: No TSVs, bumps or solder; ~0.1 pJ/bit links, with full disassembly for repair or recovery.

title: Automata Processor fixed: one hard-wired in-DRAM job, KV-cache top-k filtering
idea: Micron's Automata Processor died because nobody wanted to program NFAs and DRAM-process logic was slow. Hard-wire one function with a huge market: each bank's sense-amp stripe computes 4-bit dot products of a broadcast query against the open row of keys and returns only the indices of the top-k matches, so the accelerator fetches just those KV entries through one new command and no programming model.
why: Overfetch and data movement (facts 5, 8): long-context attention moves 10-30x less KV data off-chip, using bank-level parallelism for TB/s internal bandwidth.

title: Leaf-venation coolant network inside a glass-core interposer
idea: A glass panel replaces the silicon interposer and is laser-modified and etched with hierarchical, loop-rich vein channels modeled on dicot leaves: a midrib feeds secondary veins that feed reticulate loops under each DRAM stack and the GPU. The loops let coolant route around a blocked channel, as leaves survive insect damage.
why: Thermal limit on stack height and refresh (fact 3): glass panels cost ~2-3x less per area than silicon interposers, and embedded cooling allows taller, cooler stacks with less refresh overhead.

title: Charge-recycling buses failed on imbalance; balanced coding fixes voltage-stacked HBM lanes
idea: Charge-recycling (voltage-stacked) buses from 1990s research failed because data-dependent current imbalance between stacked lane groups collapsed the mid-rail. Split a 1,024-bit HBM bus into two stacked groups (0-0.4 V and 0.4-0.8 V) so charge spent by the upper group powers the lower, and apply DC-balanced 8b/9b-style coding per group so transitions match each cycle, leaving only a tiny mid-rail regulator.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~2x lower I/O energy by reusing each coulomb, and balanced current shrinks the decoupling needed (fewer Ta/Hf decaps); plain Si CMOS and Cu.

title: Sleep-replay consolidation: idle-time co-location of co-accessed lines
idea: During idle windows the HBM base die replays a log of recent accesses, as the hippocampus replays sequences during sleep, and physically migrates lines that were used together into the same DRAM row (with a small remap table). Later bursts become open-page hits, so one row activation serves many useful lines.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): could cut the ~5.9 pJ per useful random bit by 2-4x for recurring access patterns and lower activation counts that drive row hammer.

title: Mg: MgB2 superconducting wiring links 20 K cryogenic memory pods
idea: Run DRAM pods at ~20 K (cryocooler or liquid hydrogen) and wire them to compute with MgB2 superconducting traces (Tc 39 K, made from abundant Mg and B) on flex/interposer, so long lines are lossless and drivers swing millivolts; at 20 K access-transistor leakage collapses and refresh nearly stops.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): link energy becomes almost distance-independent (~0.1 pJ/bit) and refresh power ~0; cryo overhead must be amortized over large pods.

title: Supercritical-CO2 electroplating fills TSVs with no rinse steps
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x Cu TSV x Si x electroplating in a supercritical CO2/electrolyte emulsion. The low-viscosity emulsion penetrates high-aspect TSVs void-free and depressurizes to leave wafers dry, so the multi-stage DI rinses and spin-dries vanish; CO2 is recompressed and reused.
why: Water: plating plus rinse is a large share of TSV water, cut >10x; better high-aspect fill also lifts stack yield (fact 6).

title: Dynamics: beam-steered free-space optical links between chiplets
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics (make a fixed part adjustable): memory chiplets carry VCSEL arrays and compute chiplets carry photodiode arrays. A lid with a MEMS micromirror or liquid-crystal metasurface re-steers the beams, so any memory chiplet can be pointed at any compute tile for each workload phase.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and pooling: ~0.5-1 pJ/bit over cm distances with no interposer wiring, and idle memory is reassigned instead of over-provisioned.

title: Annular DRAM die with the GPU dropped into its hole
idea: Invert 'memory dies are rectangles with one beachfront edge': plasma-dice a DRAM die with a square hole in its center, drop the GPU die into the hole and bridge all four inner edges with short fan-out wiring.
why: Four inner edges give ~4x beachfront per memory die and uniform ~1 mm wires; ~2x bandwidth per package at lower pJ/bit than one-sided HBM placement.

title: Alignment-free z-axis film from anodized-alumina nanowires
idea: Reverse 'align pad to pad': anodize a porous alumina film (~100 nm pores at 200 nm pitch), electroplate copper nanowires through it, and laminate it between memory and logic dies; any pad overlap connects through many parallel nanowires while the alumina insulates laterally, so pitch is set by pad size, not alignment accuracy.
why: Capital: ~5 um-pitch vertical links with coarse +-2 um aligners; anodization and plating are beaker-level processes.

title: Template-grown compliant copper nanowire forest replaces hybrid bonding
idea: Grow vertical copper nanowires by electroplating through anodic-alumina pores, like crystal whiskers in a mould, on every die bond face. Each 1 um pad touches dozens of springy wires, so stacks bond at low force while tolerating 1-2 um of warp that would break hybrid bonding.
why: Raises HBM stack yield (attacks the 20-30% loss) and removes the need for CMP flatness at sub-10 nm; keeps ~1 um interconnect pitch.

title: Infrared light-through-silicon vias replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Silicon is transparent beyond 1.1 um, so a thinned DRAM stack is already an optical medium. Bond 1.3 um InGaAs micro-emitters on the base die that shine straight up through windowed metal stacks of 12 thinned dies; each tier has partially-absorbing Ge photodiode taps and electro-absorption shutters for the return path, forming vertical free-space buses with no holes drilled.
why: Eliminates TSV area (HBM uses ~3x DDR5 wafer area per bit) and TSV yield loss (20-30%) at ~0.5 pJ/bit, bringing HBM-class bandwidth near DDR5 cost per bit (fact 6).

title: Sacrificial backside allows one debond and re-thin cycle
idea: MAGNIFY reuse cycles: HBM dies keep a ~10 um sacrificial backside margin, so a debonded die can be re-thinned, re-polished and hybrid-bonded once more into a new stack.
why: Recovers known-good DRAM dies from failed or retired stacks, cutting wafer demand per shipped GB.

title: Move decoupling off the DRAM die into the interposer
idea: Rearrange where charge reservoirs live: deposit high-k ALD (HfO2/ZrO2) MIM or deep-trench capacitors in the interposer directly under each memory die's power bumps, so the DRAM die can drop most of its on-die decap.
why: Fact 7: on-die decap is several percent of the DRAM periphery; ~uF/cm2 interposer decap frees that area for bits; ALD and DRIE are routine uni-fab steps.

title: Power-line communication sends data over HBM power TSVs
idea: Adapted from home power-line networking: modulated high-frequency data is superimposed on the stack's many power/ground TSVs and planes through simple 180 nm couplers, so power vias also carry control, refresh and sideband traffic.
why: TSV count (fact 6): frees signal TSVs now spent on command and sideband, ~10-20% fewer TSVs, or more data lanes in the same footprint.
